extracted.intended_audience: scientists and technically literate readers (physicists, opticians, physicians, historians of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and desiderata for the design and assessment of photographic lenses, drawn from a historical/technical review (achromatic correction, aberration control, field flatness, aperture/speed, telephoto/portrait requirements, materials choices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfusion compatibility by agglutination testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Compatibility for human blood transfusion is determined by mixing washed donor red corpuscles with recipient sera (and vice versa) and observing whether agglutination (clumping or disintegration) occurs; agglutination in the circulating blood is undesirable as it can block vessels and cause serious trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical test: prepare serum and washed corpuscles from each donor/recipient and mix samples in test-tubes; absence of agglutination indicates compatibility. The text emphasizes that not every human blood is suitable for every recipient and that the agglutination reaction is the operative diagnostic for safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABO (von Dungern and Hirschfeld) four-group classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans may be classified into four blood groups based on two agglutinating factors in serum (a and b) and two agglutinable factors in corpuscles (A and B): Group I (neither A nor B corpuscles; serum agglutinates none), Group II (A corpuscles; serum contains b), Group III (B corpuscles; serum contains a), Group IV (A and B corpuscles; serum contains a and b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these group properties follow transfusion rules: e.g. corpuscles of Group I can be safely given only to Group I recipients; Group IV corpuscles can be given to anybody. The page gives a descriptive mapping of who can receive from whom and notes the practical importance for safe transfusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic: consider donor corpuscles and recipient serum only
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical transfusion decisions, only the qualities of the donor's corpuscles and the recipient's serum need to be considered (the other combinations are redundant for the decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: transfusing Group IV blood would theoretically agglutinate recipient corpuscles if the reaction occurred as in vitro, but in practice the transfusion is often safe—probably because the transfused plasma is too dilute to cause significant agglutination or because plasma (not serum) is injected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of blood-group reactions in disputed parentage
rubrics_metrics.description: Blood reactions can be applied to investigate cases of disputed parentage; they have limited application but give conclusive answers when applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ottenberg's work is cited as having worked out the method; the text emphasizes the method's limited but definitive utility where usable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mendelian inheritance of blood factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The blood-group qualities (A/B antigens and a/b sera) are transmitted as straightforward Mendelian factors, with consequences for compatibility among parents and offspring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: parents both of Group IV can produce only Group IV children, whereas two Group I parents may produce offspring of any group depending on hybridity; also population frequencies vary by race and region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achromatic correction (chromatic aberration control)
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental desideratum is to correct chromatic dispersion — an achromatic lens (crown+flint combination) reduces chromatic aberration and was a major early milestone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: John Dollond exhibited an achromatic prism in 1758; later lens designs build on achromatic principles. Achromatic correction remains a baseline requirement for photographic objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical aberration correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lenses should be corrected for spherical aberration, which varies with aperture and focal length and affects image quality; Huygens and Herschel provided treatments and equations for its correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers use component selection and curvature choices to control spherical aberration; some lens types correct spherical but not astigmatism and vice versa, motivating multi-glass/component designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astigmatism and distortion elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination of astigmatism and distortion is a key target; symmetry in lens design reduces astigmatism and distortion (Steinheil's insight).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Steinheil and Dallmeyer used symmetric designs and glass choices (two flints) to reduce astigmatism; Airy investigated conditions for eliminating astigmatism and distortion. Symmetry and glass-index matching are practical levers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aplanatic (coma/field) correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aplanatic correction (reducing coma and certain off-axis aberrations) is a desired property in lens components to improve off-axis image quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining components that are separately aplanatic can lead to better overall correction; the text cites work leading to 'aplanatic lenses' as a milestone in 1866.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined multi-glass designs for full correction
rubrics_metrics.description: To correct chromatic, spherical, and astigmatic errors simultaneously it may be necessary to employ three glasses (old crown, flint, and barium crown) in the components; each component can be made of all three glasses so the whole objective is achromatic, anastigmatic and aplanatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advent of new barium crown glasses made possible lenses that were achromatic, anastigmatic and aplanatic; combining two such components symmetrically yields ortho scopic lenses with flat fields (Goerz principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide correction tasks across components
rubrics_metrics.description: One practical design approach is to make one component responsible for correcting spherical aberration and another responsible for correcting astigmatism (method adopted in many Zeiss and other designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modular approach allowed designers to exploit different glass properties and component powers to tackle separate aberrations, as employed by Rudolph and early Zeiss lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petzval condition and its (sometimes optional) role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petzval condition: the sum of the power of the lenses, divided by their refractive indices, should be zero to achieve a flat anastigmatic field — a classical design condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical counterexample: some makers (Beck's Isostigmar) omitted the Petzval condition and nonetheless constructed lenses believed (and later investigated by W. Elder) to produce a flat anastigmatic field. Thus Petzval is an important guideline but designers have sometimes relaxed it with success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentric lens trade-offs (flint + barium crown)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentric lenses composed of flint and barium crown (Schroeder & Stuart) could correct astigmatism but often exhibited significant spherical aberration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers must weigh trade-offs: a configuration that improves one aberration may worsen another unless compensated by additional elements or glass types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desideratum: ortho scopic and flat-field performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A lens should ideally be ortho scopic (free from normal curvature of field) and provide a flat field of focus over the image plane for accurate reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achievable by combining appropriately corrected components symmetrically (Goerz approach) or by other multi-component designs; Cooke and Tessar families sought these properties for various applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: definition over the intended angular field at specified aperture
rubrics_metrics.description: For many applications (aerial photography, portraiture) lenses must deliver perfect or high definition over a specified (often small) angular field while operating at a particular speed (large aperture, e.g. f/5.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical example: the Air Force required a long-focus lens with perfect definition over a small angular field; Ross recalculated a lens in a fortnight to produce the 'Airo-Xpres' working at f/5.6. Designers must balance focal length, aperture (speed), and field definition requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooke lens principle: neutralising normal curvature errors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cooke (Dennis Taylor) principle: the normal curvature errors of an achromatic collective lens can be neutralised by those of an achromatic dispersive lens of the same power (made of the same glasses) placed at a suitable distance, yielding improved flat-field performance and a positive focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conceptual innovation allowed new methods of lens construction, spawning many fruitful applications (Cooke patents 1893–1898) and subsequent developments (Aviar, split-divergent designs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephoto and auxiliary front-magnifier techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Telephoto construction permits long focal lengths in a compact form (telephoto patent 1891); auxiliary magnifiers placed in front of a lens can be used (Beck's Frena camera) to modify field-of-view or effective focal length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telephoto designs and front-mounted magnifiers are accepted engineering solutions to meeting focal-length and format constraints; their optical side-effects must be accounted for in aberration correction.
